title: Stolen in the Night: How Pet Theft Feeds the Dog Meat Supply Chain
excerpt: Organised theft networks target family pets in both rural and urban Vietnam, transporting them hundreds of kilometres to informal markets. Many victims are beloved companions stolen from their homes.
body_html:
The dog meat supply chain in Vietnam runs significantly on stolen pets. Organised theft networks — some operating across multiple provinces — target family dogs in both rural villages and urban neighbourhoods, using poison bait, traps, and motorbike-mounted wire snares to capture animals quickly and quietly.

Dogs are crammed into wire mesh cages, often 10–20 animals per cage, without food, water, or veterinary care. They are then transported hundreds of kilometres to informal markets or directly to unlicensed slaughter points. By the time they arrive, many are severely dehydrated or injured.

For the families they were taken from, the loss is devastating. Dogs in Vietnam are not livestock — they are companions, protectors, and family members. The cultural and emotional bond between Vietnamese families and their dogs is precisely what makes this trade so deeply opposed by the public.

A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending the trade — a number that reflects widespread moral rejection, not fringe advocacy. The theft of family pets is cited as one of the top reasons for this overwhelming public consensus.

No registered slaughterhouse exists anywhere in Vietnam. This trade operates entirely in the shadows — and it thrives there. Sign the petition to demand accountability and a permanent ban.
